planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F, in a warm, humid, bright but shaded spot with rich, moist, well-drained soil; container culture with a winter move indoors is safest outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in warm, humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright partial shade; Malaysian Black Ginger is a compact rainforest ginger known in the wild from only a small area of the Labis Forest Reserve in Johor, Malaysia, and prized in cultivation for its glossy, deep purple-black to bronze foliage rather than for its flowers. Unlike the towering culinary and ornamental gingers, it stays compact at 2 to 5 feet, making it well suited to large containers, shaded patios, and conservatory collections outside the deep tropics. Small ground-level inflorescences open bright yellow and gradually flush pink to rose with age, providing a secondary point of interest against the near-black leaves. It demands consistent warmth, high humidity, and protection from both hot direct sun and cold drafts; in zone 9 and colder, grow it in a container and bring it indoors to a warm, bright spot before the first frost.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
National Parks Board Singapore — Flora & Fauna Web

planting.note: Plant rhizome sections with at least one growing bud 2–3 inches deep in spring in loose, moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; this species emerges later and grows considerably larger than culinary turmeric, so allow generous room and expect a longer season to rhizome maturity.

directions: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep in loose, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; Javanese Turmeric (temulawak) is native to the island of Java and is a close but distinctly larger relative of common turmeric (Curcuma longa), producing bold, paddle-shaped leaves on stems that can reach 6 to 8 feet where soil and warmth are generous — far exceeding the culinary species in scale. The showy flowering spike emerges from the base with pale-yellow true flowers tucked among pink-flushed bracts, appearing before or alongside the foliage. Throughout Indonesia and Malaysia the large, deep-orange rhizome is valued in traditional herbal tonics and beverages such as jamu, and is harvested in the same way as culinary turmeric once the foliage dies back in fall. Because it is a true lowland tropical species, it is more cold-sensitive than C. longa and performs best as a warm-season landscape feature or large container specimen outside zone 10-11.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; like other ornamental curcumas it emerges late from dormancy, so wait for consistent warmth before expecting growth.

directions: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Jewel of Burma is native to Myanmar, northeast India, and mainland Southeast Asia, where its wild habitat is increasingly threatened, making the garden trade an important refuge for the species. It is one of the most popular ornamental curcumas thanks to its dense, cone-shaped flowering spikes composed of tightly overlapping bracts in vivid orange to peach-orange tones, held above broad, light-green, dark-veined leaves that reach up to a foot long. Blooms appear from summer into fall on stems generally shorter and denser than the taller Siam tulip (C. alismatifolia), making it a good choice for containers and the front of a shaded tropical border. As with all curcumas, the foliage dies back completely in cool weather and the dormant rhizomes should be kept on the dry side until active regrowth resumes in late spring.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in an understory position with dappled to full shade, mimicking the rainforest floor where this species naturally grows.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; Australian Native Ginger is endemic to the coastal and sub-coastal rainforests of eastern Australia, ranging from the Gosford district of New South Wales north through Queensland to Cape York and the Torres Strait islands. It forms tall, arching, cane-like clumps under the rainforest canopy, with broad, glossy, alternately arranged leaves reaching well over a foot long. Unlike most gingers grown for the rhizome, the traditional bush-food harvest here is the tender white flesh at the base of the young stems, which has a mild ginger flavor, along with the bright blue, globose fruits that ripen through much of the year and were traditionally eaten fresh by Aboriginal Australians. As a true rainforest understory plant it is intolerant of dry soil, strong sun, or frost, and performs best in a consistently moist, sheltered, shaded position in zones 9b-11 or as a container specimen brought under cover in winter elsewhere.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)
